today-iowa-state-fair-crowds-ferris-whee.head: The Iowa State Fair continued through the hard years of the Great Depression.
today-iowa-state-fair-crowds-ferris-whee.body: The Iowa State Fair in Des Moines was first held in 1854, and by the 1930s it was one of the largest agricultural fairs in the country. During the Depression, many families had very little money to spend. Yet the fair carried on almost every summer. Farm families travelled to Des Moines by car, truck or train, and some camped on the fairgrounds to save money. In the great livestock barns, young members of 4-H clubs showed the calves, pigs and sheep they had raised, hoping for a blue ribbon. Women entered pies, preserves, quilts and canned vegetables in competitions. Newspapers of the time reported smaller crowds in the worst years, and prize money was sometimes reduced. Even so, the fair remained a highlight of the farming year. It offered a break from worry, a chance to meet friends, and pride in good work. Today the fair still welcomes more than a million visitors each summer, with the same barns, ribbons and Ferris wheel.
